item.title: The Manosphere Got Men Into the Gym. Now What?
item.description:
Self-Esteem

The Manosphere Got Men Into the Gym. Now What?

Men want to train, but what kind of masculinity gets built along the way?

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • For many young men, fitness is the manosphere’s front door, and it shapes how they relate to their own bodies.
  • Rather than dismissing young men’s fitness goals, adults can help their motivation mature.
  • Exercise is sustainable when it's chosen, not driven by guilt, obligation, or the need to prove yourself.
  • Training alongside men who are strong without needing to dominate can help men redefine masculinity.

For many men, the gym isn’t just training; it’s identity management. It’s one of the few places where they can reliably feel agency, strength, and self-respect.

The manosphere, a nebulous grouping of male influencers, podcasts, and content creators, has tapped into those desires, turning physical self-improvement into an entry point for creating male followers. The popularity of manosphere influencers has proven that boys and men want to be strong. That can be a good thing. But, what often happens next is more troubling.

The Slippery Slope of Manosphere Self-Improvement

In my experience, most men don’t need convincing to pay attention to their bodies. They want bodies they’re proud of. They want to feel capable, disciplined, and desirable.

The issue is how some influencers shape men's relationship with their bodies into a competition of muscle, performance, and status. Men searching for content to improve their health and fitness can easily become inundated by messages that promote obsession, perfectionism, and body dysmorphia.

Andrew Tate, the manosphere’s most notorious influencer, has said that missing one gym session won’t hurt you, but “the attitude that allows you to miss one session without guilt” will. In other words, you should feel guilty for not working out. It makes you weak—less of a man.

Two Responses That Backfire

There are two common responses to this messaging.

The first is to dismiss it as toxic nonsense. Why would you listen to someone like that?

But dismissing the manosphere misses the point. There's something men are looking for online, and shaming them for what they admire can deepen their attachment to it. We need to acknowledge the real positive changes in men who have started lifting or eating better because of manosphere influencers.

The second response is to offer a supposedly better reason to exercise: do it for others. Two years ago, I argued that men should take care of themselves not just for their own sake, but for their partners and families.

When men neglect their health, the consequences don’t stop with them. Their partners often end up carrying more of the emotional, physical, and financial burden. Self-care is, in that sense, a form of responsibility. I still believe that.

But putting all the emphasis on what a man’s fitness does for others can reinforce the expectation that a man's body doesn't really matter. It's a machine whose value lies in what it can produce. When fitness is for others, it loses its intrinsic value and becomes another performance.

The Third Path: Don’t Replace the Motive—Evolve It

What if we stopped trying to replace men’s desire to be strong and fit, and instead helped them build a healthier relationship with that motivation?

Wanting to be strong is different from believing you’re worthless when you’re weak. Wanting to be attractive is different from needing to outrank other men. Choosing discipline is different from being unable to tolerate a day of rest. The manosphere often misses all of these.

And here’s what I see most clearly in my coaching work: men may feel more comfortable treating their bodies like machines that need maintenance than companions that deserve care. It's not that men don't want to care for their bodies. It's that they've never been taught how. They've never been allowed to be more yielding, gentle, or nurturing to themselves. All they know is push, force, and domination.

What This Looks Like in Practice

If we want to help men keep fitness in their lives without dominating their bodies, measuring themselves against every man in the gym, or objectifying themselves (and others), we need to change the culture that says your worth depends on your rank, rest is weakness, and other men are competition.

If you're a man who wants to work out, ask yourself:

  • Am I training because I should, or because I want to?
  • Am I proving something, or caring for something?
  • How much of my self-worth am I attaching to my performance in the gym?

These questions help men be honest about the pressure they feel to look or perform a rigid notion of masculinity. But the work doesn't stop there. Men need other men who can model mature forms of strength and help change the narrative that strength and vulnerability are opposites.

These interactions can happen on sports teams, in running clubs, or in a well-facilitated men’s group. Or they can come from a coach, a therapist, or a friend who can say “enough” without being seen as weak. These experiences help men get comfortable with displaying strength without domination. Over time, the exercise persists and something subtle shifts:

  • Duty → Choice. “I have to train or else” makes room for “I get to do this with my body.”
  • Proving → Belonging. Training to beat other men makes room for training alongside them.
  • Self-management → Self-intimacy. Overriding pain and fatigue makes room for listening to what your body is telling you.
  • Optimization → Stewardship. Chasing better numbers makes room for caring for a body you’ll live in for decades.

None of this requires a man to stop wanting to be strong, attractive, or respected. Those desires simply no longer have to decide his worth.

For Parents, Partners, and Clinicians

If a young man in your life is watching this content, try asking what about these influencers resonates with him. What do they seem to understand about his life that other adults miss? Is it discipline? A sense of purpose? Men to look up to?

Honor that motive. Then help him find a healthier place to pursue it.

He already wants to work out. What gets built next is the whole story.

item.title: Why You Treat Your Future Self Like a Stranger
item.description:
Procrastination

Why You Treat Your Future Self Like a Stranger

How caring more about your future self can reduce stress.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • We often make choices that benefit us today but create problems for us later.
  • Research suggests we sometimes treat our future selves as if they were strangers.
  • Feeling more connected to the person we'll become can reduce procrastination and encourage better decisions.

Do you care about yourself and want the best for yourself? Most people would say yes. But that isn’t how we treat ourselves, especially a specific aspect of ourselves—our future self.

The evidence for that isn’t hard to find. You drink too much and wake up with a headache and a hangover. You push off an unpleasant task and have to deal with it the following week. You spend too much money and then stress out about paying next month’s bills. You skip the gym and eat foods you know are bad for you and saddle your future self with health problems. In short, we are pretty inconsiderate today of the person we’ll be tomorrow, and unsurprisingly, research confirms that we actually treat ourselves no better than we would a stranger.

Why We Treat Our Future Selves Like Strangers

In one study, participants were told they would have to drink a terrible-tasting liquid either immediately or later in the semester and were asked to decide how much they would drink. Those who chose to drink it immediately agreed to down about two tablespoons. Those choosing to drink it later sign on for half a cup—far more than they were willing to drink that day. When participants were asked how much of the unpleasant brew they would assign a stranger to drink, they chose about half a cup again.

This is why we postpone unpleasant tasks, ignore future consequences, and make decisions that saddle us with problems later—because we treat our future selves like strangers. But we can change that.

Make Friends With Your Future Self

Another study found that people behaved differently toward their future selves when they felt more connected to the person they would become. Participants were shown computer-generated images of what their faces might look like in a few decades and then decided how much money to allocate to their retirement savings. Those who saw their faces digitally aged allocated more money than those who did not. Seeing the image made the future version of themselves feel more real, and that helped participants consider their long-term well-being.

I was excited when I first read these studies because this is something I’ve been doing for many years without knowing there was research behind it. How I do it might sound silly—mostly because it is—but I’ve found it remarkably useful. Whenever I catch myself about to postpone an unpleasant task, I say to myself: That’s going to make next week harder for Next-Week-Guy. Don’t do that to him. Or, Tomorrow-Guy will be very grateful if I take care of this now. And then when the next day or week arrives, and the task is already done, I take a moment to thank the earlier version of myself for taking care of it and freeing me from the burden, even if it’s small.

So yes, I’m having imaginary conversations with my future self, but doing that makes that version of me feel more real, and that helps me act with greater consideration for him. It’s especially useful for things like procrastination. Postponing tasks doesn’t eliminate the stress of doing them, and it often increases it when an unpleasant task that could have been completed in a few minutes today becomes a source of worry for days or weeks. Being considerate of the person you’ll be later and doing them the favor of taking the unpleasant task of their shoulders also spares them (you) unnecessary stress.

Three Ways to Build a Better Relationship With Your Future Self

1. Give them an identity. Instead of thinking vaguely about doing something “later,” picture the person who will have to deal with it. Call them Tomorrow-You, Next-Week-You, or use your own name (I use tomorrow-Guy or next-year-Guy). The more real that person feels, the more you will care about them and want to make life easier and better for them.

2. Consider the consequences for them. When you’re about to postpone something, ask yourself: How will I feel about having to do this under pressure because now it’s urgent? Or, What if other important things come in and having to do this next week becomes really stressful? You might still decide to postpone it, but considering the consequences might motivate you to do it now.

3. Thank your past self. When you benefit from something you did earlier—doing the unpleasant task, packing for the trip ahead of time, or skipping the dessert you were kind of too full to have anyway—take a moment to acknowledge it. Thanks for taking care of me, Yesterday-Guy. It might feel strange at first, but having a better relationship with your future self and treating that version of yourself like a friend instead of a stranger can make your life easier and it can make you happier and healthier.

We usually think of self-care as something we do in the present, like relaxing, exercising, or taking a break. But I believe that some of the most valuable acts of self-care are actually acts of kindness toward our future selves. And they will be very grateful to you for it.

Adapted from Mind Over Grind: How to Break Free When Work Hijacks Your Life (Simon & Schuster, 2026).

item.title: What Your Team Stops Telling You When Founders Fight
item.description:
Career

What Your Team Stops Telling You When Founders Fight

Cofounder conflict pushes problems out of sight until they blow up later.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Teams pick up tension between founders through tone, interruptions and silence.
  • Employees often side with the founder who holds more power, to protect themselves.
  • Agreeing when an employee vents about your cofounder strengthens the back channel.
  • Repair starts with the founders realigning before trying to change the team.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

Nobody said a word about last week's fight with your cofounder. They don't need to. In Monday's all-hands meeting, your team watched you interrupt him. They watched him shut down, and they saw the look on his face. And now they're censoring what they will tell you directly and what they will say behind your back.

One pair of founders I worked with agreed with each other in private. In team meetings, one of them kept undercutting the other in front of the people they'd hired. When the first founder corrected someone's technical work, his cofounder called it micromanagement. Neither of them described what that word meant to them.

The team heard it as permission to ignore the feedback. The first founder became "the difficult one," and people stopped listening to him. He told me, "I feel like my rights are taken away."

His cofounder thought he was protecting the team from harshness. The team learned that the founders weren't aligned, and one of them could be ignored.

What a Team Picks Up From Its Founders

People read body language and feel tension between others even when nobody names it.

In a meeting, they notice who interrupts whom, who questions whom and in what tone, and whether one founder has withdrawn. The more often the two of you fight, the louder those signals get. It shows up in the work. One of you hands someone a task. Then the other tells them it's the wrong priority, and the work gets redone.

Founders' moods carry extra weight. You hold status and power. People idealize you, mostly without realizing it. In my experience, many employees start to relate to a founder the way they once related to a parent or to whoever held power in their lives.

In Emotional Contagion (1994), Elaine Hatfield and colleagues described how emotions spread through groups. People pick up and mirror the feelings of those around them. Later work on teams by Thomas Sy and others (2005) found that a leader's mood spreads to the group and affects how well the group coordinates. When two founders are tense in a meeting, the room tends to stay tense after they leave.

Think about children whose parents are fighting. The kids often don't know what the fight is about, and they feel it anyway. They notice the tone at dinner and the door that shuts a little too hard. They can't fix it and they can't leave, because they depend on both parents.

So they adapt. Some drift toward anxiety and some act out. Others take a side, try to become the peacemaker, or shut down. A team is in a similar spot. Their paychecks and much of their identity are tied to the two of you. And they have far less control over the company's future than you do.

How Employees End Up Choosing a Side

When people can't fix the tension above them, many seek connection to whichever founder keeps them safest.

Say the CEO has been hinting that the CTO is underperforming. If I'm an employee, it makes sense to get closer to the CEO, because she holds more power. I'll keep feeding her information and try to learn how she thinks. I'll keep the CTO happy on the surface, but stop giving him honest feedback.

The psychiatrist Murray Bowen, in the family systems theory he developed from the 1950s through the 1970s, called this triangulation. When tension between two people gets too high, a third person gets pulled in to absorb some of it. That takes attention off the original conflict, so the conflict between the two founders stays frozen.

I often think about the people who often get pulled in to mediate conflict between founders as parentified employees—the emotionally intelligent individuals wired for caretaking. They often end up in Head of People, HR, or Chief of Staff roles. Being the go-between can feel good at first. It tells an employee, "I'm valued here. I'm important." It also pulls their attention away from their own work, and tends to raise their anxiety.

Founders can feed this dynamic without noticing. An employee comes to you frustrated with your cofounder. You're frustrated with him too, so you sigh, agree and maybe add a story of your own. This provides temporary relief from the tension and helps you and the employee feel closer, but it prevents your cofounder from hearing the friction necessary for change. Icing him out reinforces the narrative that he is not to be respected, and accelerates the chances of his eventual departure. What would be far more helpful is coaching the employee to take the feedback to your cofounder directly.

Repair Starts With the Two of You

Startup Snapshot studied startup employee wellbeing. Employees whose founder was highly stressed reported 14% higher burnout. Cofounder conflict disrupts your ability to focus and execute, and negatively impacts your employees. The longer you fight, the higher the risk of churn your company faces.

Get realigned with your cofounder before you try to fix anything on the team. With the pair above, I started by bringing attention to the word that kept causing damage. I asked them to define micromanagement together and to stop using it as a weapon in front of the team. Then, I suggested they increase their frequency of operational syncs so they could enter meetings fully aligned.

After you've made initial progress with your cofounder, show the team the culture you want. Your team copies what you do, so let them see you disagree, work it out, and commit to a decision. Because of the power gap, that alone won't give most employees the same freedom to push back. So ask for it directly, and when it comes, handle it well.

The next time someone vents to you about your cofounder, ask whether they've told your cofounder directly, and help them figure out how they could. That small shift can help contain conflict so it doesn't contaminate your execution.

item.title: When Elephants Grieve, What Are They Thinking and Feeling?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

When Elephants Grieve, What Are They Thinking and Feeling?

Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor explain the profound effects of loss.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • It’s essential to recognize and honor grief in elephants and other animals.
  • An elephant's death can affect an entire social world: relationships may be disrupted and knowledge lost.
  • Death must be factored into conservation decisions, human-wildlife conflict, and the care of captive animals.
  • Our inability to fully understand another species' emotional life isn't evidence that it is absent.
An extended elephant family gathers to drink at Mushara waterhole in Etosha National Park, Namibia, on a July evening in 2025.
Source: Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor.

There's little doubt that elephants and many other animals experience grief. Elephants often are the "poster animals" for their profound response to the death of other elephants, something I observed after the death of an elephant matriarch in the Samburu National Reserve along with elephant expert Dr. Iain Douglas-Hamilton. I could literally feel their grief and the depth of their loss. Psychologists Drs. Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor's research on this important topic speaks to many current questions of interest about this important and hot topic.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you decide to study grief in elephants?

Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor: Our interest in elephant grief grew from our work as psychologists and our longstanding curiosity about the emotional lives of animals. Much of our professional work has centered on grief, attachment, and the ways people navigate loss, including the loss of beloved companion animals. Through this work, we've come to appreciate that grief is, in many ways, a reflection of love and attachment. It speaks to the significance of relationships.

That led us to ask: If grief emerges from attachment, memory, and the disruption of social bonds, why assume it is exclusively human?

Elephants are especially compelling because of their complex, multigenerational societies, enduring relationships, and remarkable communication. Our interest deepened through our connection with Dr. Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell and a visit to Mushara, a research waterhole in Namibia's Etosha National Park. Witnessing elephants interact in their natural environment was profoundly moving.

Our work draws on decades of field research to explore what elephant responses to death might reveal about attachment, memory, and loss. That said, scientific humility is essential: each species must be understood within its own biological, social, and ecological context.

MB: Who do you hope to reach with your research?

DK/KL: People who have never considered that wildlife might respond to loss in ways resembling grief. Many of us readily recognize the attachments of dogs and cats, yet don't always extend that understanding to wild animals.

We also hope to reach psychologists, educators, conservationists, and policymakers. For conservation, protecting elephants means more than maintaining population numbers. It also means considering family structures, relationships, and knowledge passed between generations.

Most importantly, we hope readers will see animals through a more compassionate and thoughtful lens. The more we understand their social lives, the harder it becomes to regard them solely as populations to manage. Greater understanding can inspire not only empathy, but also a deeper sense of responsibility for how we coexist with other species.

Members of an elephant family gather to drink at the head of the trough at Mushara, a waterhole within a research area closed to the public in Namibia’s Etosha National Park. Elephant families often compete for access to this preferred drinking location, where the water is freshest.
Source: Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor.

MB: What are some of your major findings and major messages?

DK/KL: One striking finding is elephants' sustained interest in the dead. Researchers have observed them touching bodies with their trunks, investigating bones, remaining near remains, and sometimes revisiting death sites. These behaviors suggest that death has social and behavioral significance beyond the immediate moment.

Equally important is the complexity of elephant relationships. Families depend on communication, memory, and intergenerational learning. The death of a matriarch can mean not only the loss of an individual, but also the loss of ecological knowledge that helps others survive.

Elephant brain structures associated with memory and social-emotional processing offer relevant biological context, although anatomy alone cannot establish what an elephant feels. And elephants are not alone: researchers have observed potentially grief-related responses to death in chimpanzees, orcas, and other species. Such observations are studied within comparative thanatology, the interdisciplinary study of how animals respond to death.

Our central message is that an elephant's death can affect an entire social world: relationships may be disrupted, knowledge lost, and surviving animals profoundly affected.

MB: How does your work differ from others concerned with these topics?

DK/KL: We see our contribution as complementary to the work of field biologists, ethologists, and neuroscientists. Their observations provide the essential evidence. We bring those findings into conversation with psychology, grief research, and animal ethics.

In particular, we ask what our understanding of attachment and bereavement might help us recognize in other species, while remaining cautious about direct comparisons. We also ask what ethical responsibilities follow when research shows that animals maintain lasting relationships and experience social disruption following death.

What should that mean for conservation decisions, human-wildlife conflict, and the care of elephants in captivity? We hope to honor the contributions of field researchers by making these questions accessible and relevant to how we understand and treat other animals.

MB: Are you hopeful that, as people learn about grief in elephants and other animals, they will use this information on behalf of the animals?

DK/KL: Absolutely. How we understand animals influences how we treat them.

Conservation has rightly emphasized habitat protection and population survival. But with highly social species, numbers tell only part of the story. An elephant killed by poachers may also be a mother, a companion, or a matriarch carrying decades of ecological knowledge. Her death may have consequences throughout the group. Likewise, caring for elephants in captivity requires attention not only to physical health, but also to social relationships and opportunities for natural behavior.

We hope this research encourages greater humility, curiosity, and compassion. Rather than judging animals by how closely they resemble humans, we can ask how they experience their own worlds.

Recognizing the possibility of grief in elephants does not require us to say their experience is identical to ours. It asks us to take their relationships seriously. If our work helps even a few people see an elephant as an individual with relationships, memories, and a life that matters, then it has accomplished something meaningful. Ultimately, we hope understanding animals' emotional lives will inspire us to treat them with the dignity and respect they deserve.

item.title: How the 4 Cs Destroy Intimacy and How You Can Repair It
item.description:
Relationships

How the 4 Cs Destroy Intimacy and How You Can Repair It

Criticism, complaining, controlling, and complacency erode emotional safety.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Intimacy is a fragile agreement based on trust, safety, and security.
  • Partners need to carve out time to discuss how mundane interactions may be unintentionally landing.
  • Couples often need guidance on how to communicate authentically and compassionately, even when they disagree.

Many couples come into my office believing that their conflicts are about mundane things, such as who should load the dishwasher or how to reduce their credit card bills, and many of them learn that the real underlying problems are trust, safety, and security. Intimacy is a fragile agreement that is renewed daily, and the signifiers that are read subconsciously by both partners can cause them to feel disrespected and unsupported, which destroys the desire to be intimate.

In his book Role Mate to Soul Mate, relationship expert Dr. Warren Farrell argues that four relatively normal yet bad habits — criticism, complaining, controlling, and complacency — are detrimental to intimacy long before either partner notices that the relationship has grown stale. I love how Dr. Farrell provides a practical map of exactly where the erosion begins (earlier than you think) for couples as well as the clinicians who work with them.

Each of what Dr. Farrell calls “the Four Cs” operates through a distinct psychological mechanism that subtly provides the recipient with a subconscious reason to pull back:

  • Criticism unintentionally attacks identity rather than behavior, so the recipient hears a character assassination and responds with the same defensiveness that would arise from any threat to survival, shutting down the very openness that intimacy requires.
  • Complaining broadcasts dissatisfaction, leaving the listener with no real actionable path toward repair and only the odd sense that they have disappointed someone and are not “good-enough.” This often breeds a quiet, hopeless withdrawal and/or complacency.
  • Complacency operates more slowly than the others (and I think it can be even more insidious). It teaches partners, through years of unremarked effort, that their contributions aren’t appreciated. This lack of appreciation is corrosive in a way that even open conflict is not, because it eliminates the positive reinforcement necessary to keep a person offering anything at all. Here the withdrawal of intimacy is a rational response to an environment that has come to feel — however subtly — emotionally unsafe.
  • Controlling language communicates distrust and informs the partner that their judgment is considered unreliable. The natural reaction to being micromanaged is to conceal rather than share, since concealment feels like agency and autonomy.

I worked with a couple in which the husband was very adept at complimenting his wife on her domestic competence while saying very little about the marriage itself — she would say that he was polite but that he had low EQ. By the time they came to me, she described feeling more like a competent maid (or his mother) than a partner. Her subconscious response was to lose interest in being intimate because of this dynamic that he unwittingly established: not appreciating her as a person, but just for the tasks she performed. She wanted to be appreciated for her beauty, intellect, being fun, and being a good mother, and not just for maintaining a clean house. Actually, with the best intentions, the husband’s positive reinforcement for cleaning landed with the wife as “controlling.” It appeared that the husband had a subconscious imprint of gender roles in his head, and his expectations only rewarded his wife when she behaved accordingly. Dr. Farrell believes that damage can accumulate even when nothing overtly dramatic appears to be happening, and this is what I have witnessed in sessions with couples.

Over the past eighteen years as a clinician, I have seen over and over how criticism, complaining, controlling, and complacency can destroy intimacy. Couples usually need guidance on how to communicate authentically and compassionately with each other, and this usually requires blocking out time and framing weekly “Caring and Sharing” sessions outside of therapy, as Dr. Farrell suggests. Once each partner knows there is time set aside each week to make each of them feel fully heard — even if they disagree with each other — the “walking on eggshells” and emotional distance are replaced by feeling more emotionally safe, secure, connected, deeply in love, free to be vulnerable, and thus more intimate. Books such as Role Mate to Soul Mate provide tools to help couples identify their criticism, complaining, controlling, and complacency and make changes to rebuild love and intimacy.

item.title: Build a Career Around Being Yourself
item.description:
Career

Build a Career Around Being Yourself

Look at your performance and results, and try to discern patterns.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Peter Drucker was a master at expressing his uniqueness in a career spanning more than 70 years.
  • Expressing what makes us unique requires being genuine, sincere, and authentic.
  • Make a lists of areas of strength that can transcend disciplines and be applied to a variety of roles.
  • Apply your areas of excellence to help others in their self-discovery process.
Source: Anton Vierietin/Shutterstock

We are living through an era of doubts about what constitutes reality, and trepidation about the effects AI will have on jobs and livelihoods. That leads to an important question: how can you build a career around being yourself?

Peter Drucker, the father of modern management (1909-2005), was a master at tapping into his own uniqueness while encouraging people to examine what made them unique and valuable to others. Nearly sixty years ago, in his classic book The Effective Executive, he wrote that “the effective executive tries to be himself; he does not pretend to be someone else. He looks at his own performance and at his own results and tries to discern a pattern.”

Consider what made Drucker unique. Many people, then and now, engaged in the same activities as his: writing, teaching, and consulting. But nobody did it quite like him, and it is why people worldwide continue to pay attention to what he wrote, taught, and advised.

Over a period of many years, people wanted to be in Drucker’s presence, either when he gave presentations and keynotes, lectures in classes and at conferences, or in one-on-one meetings, especially for his consulting clients. They wanted access to his mind, not only for in-person activities, but in the numerous books and articles he wrote in a career spanning more than 70 years.

Expressing What Makes Us Unique and Valuable

We can strive for similar attention and effects, even though we are unlikely to have the same magnitude, as we express our individuality in daily activities and planning for the future. Making the most of being yourself is a deceptively simple concept, yet is not necessarily easy to carry out.

We can work on how we express what makes us unique and valuable in our own lives and work, and how we interact with other people. It means being genuine, sincere, and authentic, with a positive and resourceful attitude.

Being the most complete expression of yourself helps you to avoid the trap of comparing yourself to others, or engaging in unhelpful thoughts like impostor syndrome, with the nagging feeling that you don’t deserve or belong in your role. Taking advantage of, and looking for the fullest expression of our individuality and its potential requires self-awareness, confidence, high quality, and self-efficacy.

Listing Areas of Strength

If you want to build a career revolving around being yourself, make and review lists of areas of strength that can transcend disciplines and be applied to a variety of roles, and not just one particular job.

For example, here are ten examples of personal/professional excellence qualities:

  • Listening
  • Empathy
  • Creativity
  • Curiosity
  • Learning
  • Teaching
  • The search for and discovery of knowledge
  • Problem-solving
  • Subject matter expertise
  • Leadership

Everyone will have their own unique list, based on personal interests and experience; and talents they were born with, or developed early or later in life.

These areas of excellence can still be strengthened in the future. Being yourself does not mean remaining static; like Drucker, you should be open to change and to engage in self-development as you move into an uncertain future. One reason he remained at the top of his various professions for so many years is that he engaged in regular and fairly rigorous self-study projects (from world history to the works of Shakespeare). Everyone is a work in progress.

Conclusion: Becoming More Human

Being aware of our human strengths can also help other people to take advantage of being themselves. For instance, many of the examples of personal excellence listed above (e.g. listening, empathy and compassion, teaching, and leadership) lend themselves to collaborating with others to aid in their own self-discovery process.

“To be a leader today,” the leadership coach and author Hortense le Gentil recently wrote, “is not to compete with the machine. It is to become more human. To do the things that cannot be coded or digitized. Sure, we can tell AI to write with more empathy and compassion. But the output remains a simulation of human emotion.”

Generative AI is awe-inspiring. In the past four years, we’ve witnessed astonishing achievements. Yet AI can’t copy exactly what we do, who we are, or what makes us unique. How can we maintain and continue to develop that advantage, with AI’s inevitable improvements in the future?

item.title: How to Support a Child Interested in STEM
item.description:
Education

How to Support a Child Interested in STEM

STEM classes are hard. Parent support can help kids succeed.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional support has physiological and emotional benefits and can be provided with limited STEM knowledge.
  • Showing up, listening, reaching out, and making an effort goes a long way in helping women succeed in STEM.
  • Parental advice that is clear, relevant to a child's interests, and concrete was appreciated by STEM majors.
Source: YY TEOH/Unsplash

Research study after research study shows the importance of parent and family support for sparking kids’ interests in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) and then helping them stay interested and succeed in STEM as they grow. But how exactly do parents provide helpful support?

A recent study from my team of researchers at Michigan State University (Dorrance Hall et al., 2025) reports on how parents support girls pursuing STEM and women majoring in STEM in college. We interviewed Black, Latina, and white women majoring in STEM across the United States and asked them about the STEM-related support they received while growing up. The findings identify five ways parents can provide much-needed support throughout childhood and adolescence.

1. Advice

Advice, or instrumental support, was the most commonly reported type of support received from parents. Parental advice was useful for navigating important decisions like choosing a major and career path. Parents suggested majors and careers, told girls how to apply for college, provided study tips, and shared job and internship postings. Women appreciated advice that was clear, relevant to their interests, and concrete as opposed to general. They disliked advice that focused on what the parents wanted them to do over their own interests.

2. Resources

Another major way parents can support their children’s interests in STEM is to provide resources such as STEM books and materials, enroll them in after-school activities, and take them to museums. Women reflected on more surprising forms of support that do not cost a lot of money as well—things like cooking meals for them so they could focus on their homework, giving them rides to and from classes, and investing their time to help with challenging assignments.

3. Comfort and empathy

Parents can provide comfort, empathy, and emotional support as they cope with the challenges of pursuing STEM. Challenges, such as feeling like they don’t belong in their classes or activities and not seeing themselves as scientists in online representations (just to name a few), are amplified for women and people in other underrepresented groups. Children in these groups likely need additional support to succeed in STEM.

Fortunately, there are a lot of ways parents can provide emotional support, starting with comfort and empathy. Emotional support has physiological and emotional health benefits, and parents can provide it even if they have very limited knowledge about STEM. Simply validating that STEM is hard and that the challenges their children are facing are stressful can go a long way. Parents can also help their children gain perspective by reminding them why they are pursuing STEM, that grades only matter so much, and that a semester or school year is temporary. Parents can talk about their children’s skills and their confidence in their kids’ ability to succeed.

4. Encouragement and affirmations

Similar to emotional support, parents can encourage and affirm their children’s strengths by providing esteem support. To do this, parents can express pride in their kids’ accomplishments, remind them they are smart, and show them they believe in them to boost their confidence. This type of support can improve self-esteem and well-being and protect against self-doubt.

5. Social connections

Parents can also help their children network with others and teach them to ask for help when they need it. Women shared that their parents used their networks to introduce them to new opportunities or help them find the information they needed when the parents did not personally know how to help them. Parents found other adults who had firsthand knowledge about the industry their child was interested in or showed their children how to ask others for help.

Women majoring in STEM described a lot of different things their parents said or did as supportive. This shows that parents have a lot of choice when it comes to how to best support their child. There was not a one-size-fits-all way to be supportive. Instead, parents should stay attuned to what their child needs at their current developmental stage and think about what would be most helpful for the specific challenges they are facing.

Parents can improve their support by making their advice specific and relevant to their child. This could look like saying, “I remember you telling me you were interested in learning about the different types of engineering. Let’s check out these programs that introduce kids to a wide variety of things engineers can do.”

Even if the support a parent gives is not exactly what is needed at the time, women in our study told us that the simple act of receiving support was helpful. Parents showing up, listening, reaching out, and making an effort go a long way in helping women succeed in STEM.

item.title: The Link Between Youth Loneliness and Smartphone Dependency
item.description:
Adolescence

The Link Between Youth Loneliness and Smartphone Dependency

Loneliness and technology are shaping youth mental health and connection.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness can intensify the relationship between smartphone dependency and mental health challenges.
  • Increased social media use during the pandemic was linked to higher stress, anxiety, and depression.
  • AI chatbots can simulate emotional connections, potentially increasing unhealthy technology dependence.
  • Therapy can help youth rebuild social skills, emotional regulation, and meaningful real-world connections.
Source: Keenan Constance / Unsplash

by Dante Lewis-Chan and Robert T. Muller, Ph.D.

According to the 2023 Canadian Health Survey on Children and Youth, the rate of adolescents with poor mental health had more than doubled between 2019 and 2023. The survey assessed mental well-being in 2019, and checked in with those same participants four years later. In the initial survey, about 12 percent of youth aged 12 to 17 had rated their mental health as “fair” or “poor.” This figure rose to 26 percent by 2023.

After the survey’s initial assessment, the COVID-19 pandemic had started. During the pandemic, screen time rose across all age groups. A 2024 study examined this rise and found that students who used social media to cope with the pandemic experienced higher levels of stress, anxiety, and depression. However, this relationship was more pronounced amongst lonelier students.

These findings were echoed in a 2025 study conducted in China. Loneliness, this study found, intensified the relationship between social anxiety and smartphone overdependence in college students. This is further supported by a recent review that suggests a strong association between feelings of isolation and an over-reliance on smartphones.

Jake Ernst, a social worker and psychotherapist in Toronto, explains how chronic loneliness can lead to mental health issues: “For young people, whose brains are still building the scaffolding required for social connection, isolation interrupts the development of essential skills like executive functioning, emotional regulation, and conflict repair."

Ernst also believes that smartphone dependency plays a role in isolation and exacerbates these challenges. He describes it as a paradox: Technology can offer the illusion of connection while actually displacing meaningful, real-world contact. Many young people now spend their time in online spaces, prioritising attention and comparison over genuine connection and weakening their ability to handle real-world social challenges. As they turn more to curated digital interactions instead of practicing real communication, their dependence on these platforms only grows stronger.

Another growing concern in the discussion around youth loneliness is artificial intelligence. There is an emerging phenomenon of people forming emotional and romantic connections with AI. The consequences of such interactions can be alarming, particularly for youth already struggling with their mental health.

Source: Tasha Kostyuk / Unsplash

A Stanford study conducted in 2025 found that with some commonly used chatbots, like character.ai and Replika, one can elicit inappropriate dialogue concerning topics like self-harm, drug use, and violence. The study notedthat this is especially dangerous for young people, as they are not fully developed and so are more likely to form attachments, even with an AI chatbot.

Chatbots can simulate deep, complex relationships, and while youth recognize that AI isn’t necessarily “alive,” it doesn’t stop them from reciprocating. “AI has mostly intensified smartphone dependency by personalizing it,” Ernst claims. “AI-driven chatbots and companion apps now simulate friendship, intimacy, or care, but without the reciprocity that real relationships require.”

Ernst believes therapeutic interventions can be effective to treat smartphone dependency in youth, as long as “the social health deficit and the digital over-reliance” are addressed. He notes that therapy offers opportunities to develop the ability to co-regulate and process emotions in real-time. It also provides real-world experiences that allow youth to “rediscover the positive aspects of life,” and train the parts of their brains that require those experiences for healthy development.

It can be easy for young people to self-isolate and fall into unhealthy or destructive relationships with technology. But with the right interventions and support from in-person relationships, young people struggling with smartphone dependency can be helped. They can rebuild their sense of connection, regain their social skills, reset their brains, and change their view of the world, both digital and real.

Dante Lewis-Chan is a research student at York University.

item.title: You Can See Everything on the Surface, Not What Lies Beneath
item.description:
Motivation

You Can See Everything on the Surface, Not What Lies Beneath

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary has audiences fascinated by her behavior.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Behavior is what we see on the surface. It tells only the outer layer of the story.
  • Hidden drivers, often formed in childhood, steer all of us, usually without our noticing.
  • Every driver has a shadow side. The danger isn't having one; it's refusing to see it.

I’m writing from the Hamptons. It’s the off-season, and the place feels like a small town, albeit a small town full of influential people, big thinkers, and, yes, some big egos. Almost everyone here is talking about You Can See Everything.

“Do you believe her? Aren’t her eyes crazy? Is she a narcissist? And what about her partner? Was he the real villain?”

It’s human nature to sort people into categories. We want to figure out what happened, so we won’t get fooled ourselves. We want a villain and a victim. We also want to feel better about ourselves, because at least we’re not “that crazy.” And it makes good theater.

If you haven’t seen the film: In the 34 days before Elizabeth Holmes reported to federal prison, she and her partner, Billy Evans, let a film crew led by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim record nearly every move. On the surface, the goal seemed to be showing them as everyday parents: raising their kids, walking on the beach, making eggs.

The title makes a promise: full access, nothing hidden, the real person behind the headlines at last.

The movie is disorienting. It took me a while to process. I won’t share all my thoughts here, but one has stayed with me: A camera can see everything on the surface. It can’t see the hidden drivers underneath.

A camera records behavior: what we say, how we stand, the stories we tell. It rarely captures the why. Under every polished performance and every bad decision, a hidden driver is steering. Unless you’re looking for it, you’ll miss it.

In my work as an executive coach, I use an assessment that uncovers these drivers and lays out the good, the bad, and the ugly in each one. I didn’t create it, and to be clear, it isn’t a personality test. It measures drive: the deep needs that push us forward.

I’ve never assessed Elizabeth Holmes, and I won’t guess at what drives her. But I have coached many founders and tech leaders, and her story reminds me of one of them. She happens to be a woman, but many men fall into the same trap. Her story shows what happens when hidden drivers go unseen.

A Cautionary Case Study

A few years ago, I was asked to assess the hidden drivers of a senior leader. I’ll call her Laura*. That isn’t her name, and I’ve changed other details to protect her privacy.

From a distance, Laura had it all. She was brilliant, fast-moving, and, on paper, wildly successful. She carried herself as if she were the only one in the know and everyone else was slow to catch up.

When you asked her a question, she didn’t answer it. She used the moment to show how much more she knew. I could see why the people around her stopped asking questions. Nobody wants to feel stupid.

Her assessment results explained why. They showed two strong hidden drivers.

The first was going it alone. Somewhere in childhood, Laura’s brain had learned a rule: I can only count on myself. Needing anyone makes me weak.

The second was winning. Second place was not an option.

Put the two together, and her behavior makes sense. Being the smartest person in the room kept Laura in charge. If she always knew better, she never had to need anyone. And every conversation became a contest she could win.

As executive coach Marshall Goldsmith puts it, “Half the leaders I have met don’t need to learn what to do. They need to learn what to stop.”

Laura had built a life where she never had to need anyone. The cost was that no one could truly reach her: not her team, not even her best friend.

I see this pairing of drivers in high-performing leaders all the time. In many ways, it’s what got them to the top. But every driver has a shadow side.

People driven to go it alone tend to keep information to themselves, especially information that makes them look bad. People driven to win have trouble knowing a battle worth fighting from one that’s costing everyone around them.

I sat down with Laura and gently walked her through her results. I told her what her drivers were giving her and what they might cost her.

She listened. Then she said, “I’d like to take the test again.”

I told her the truth: It doesn’t work that way. A hidden driver isn’t a mood that changes depending on how you slept. It’s more like the foundation of a house. You can repaint the walls and rearrange the furniture, but the foundation stays where it was poured.

Here’s what I didn’t say out loud: Her request for a re-test was her drivers at work. To someone driven to go it alone, feedback sounds like “You need help.” To someone driven to win, a hard result feels like losing. So, she did what her drivers had always taught her to do. She tried to beat the test instead of learning from it.

That moment was a choice point: a small gap between what happened and what she did next. In that gap, Laura could have gotten curious. Instead, she reverted to the comfort of her drivers on autopilot.

A few years later, I heard that Laura had lost everything due to her own pride and arrogance: her company, her investors, her own money, and her reputation. I wasn’t surprised. Without awareness, there’s no way to change. Left unchecked, any of us can sabotage ourselves.

I’ve worked with other leaders who share Laura’s drivers and did change. They learned to reflect on themselves and take responsibility for their behavior. Laura never did.

Understanding the Science

Patterns begin in childhood. Attachment researchers have studied Laura’s pattern for decades. John Bowlby, the father of attachment theory, described people who become “compulsively self-reliant.” Adults with this pattern tend to hide or play down their feelings so they won’t look vulnerable, weak, or dependent on others.

Think of it like this: A child who learns that needing people isn’t safe builds a suit of armor. The armor protects the child. But decades later, the adult is still wearing it and wonders why no one can get close.

Fear makes everyone go quiet. Laura’s need to look smart came with a hidden price. Research on harsh bosses has found that abusive supervision makes employees afraid, and fear leads them to go silent. Harvard’s Amy Edmondson, who studies what she calls psychological safety, found that when it was missing, people were less willing to speak up, ask for help, or admit mistakes, so teams learned less.

Bad news stops traveling upward. Psychologists call this the “Mum Effect.” People tend to soften or hold back bad news, especially when it must go to someone powerful. Stanford professor Robert Sutton described a chilling example. After the 1986 Challenger disaster, physicist Richard Feynman found that NASA’s working engineers put the chance of losing a shuttle at roughly 1 in 100. NASA’s managers put it at 1 in 100,000. The truth had been softened at every step on its way up.

Now put the pieces together. Laura hid her own bad news about her failing company because her self-reliance wouldn’t let her look weak. Her team hid their bad news because she made them feel stupid for speaking up. She ended up leading from inside a bubble where nobody told her the truth, not even herself.

Her drivers weren’t what brought her down. Not seeing them was.

Understanding Hidden Drivers Is Not Excusing

Let me be clear: Seeing someone’s hidden drivers doesn’t let them off the hook. Laura was responsible for how she treated people, and Elizabeth Holmes was convicted for what she did.

But labels like “bully,” “fraud,” or “villain” close the case. They let us feel safely different from the person we’re judging. Understanding drivers keeps the case open, and that makes change possible. You can’t change what you can’t see.

Seeing your hidden drivers isn’t a label or a verdict. It’s a mirror. And unlike Laura, you don’t need a re-test. You just need the willingness to look.

The Part No Camera Can Film

You Can See Everything promises full access. But none of us can see everything: not in a famous founder, not in the person across the table, and not in ourselves. Not without help and honesty.

All of us have a shadow side. Elizabeth Holmes’s story is an extreme one, but it’s a reminder of how much denial and ego can cost. Whether you’re in over your head at work or hiding the truth from people you care about, you're standing at a choice point. You can dig in deeper, or you can ask for help: from a therapist, a coach, or a trusted friend. Someone who can hold up a mirror and tell you what they see.

You can’t see everything. But you can learn to see yourself.

item.title: The Mustache Was Never the Point of Movember
item.description:
Friends

The Mustache Was Never the Point of Movember

Movember started as a dare between friends. That's exactly why it works.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Building friendships take time that can start with a cause.
  • Causes can give you a common connection point.
  • Showing up is just as important as sharing your feelings, if not more so.
  • Sign up for something slightly ridiculous to have a good story to tell.
The author and friends doing ridiculous things
Source: Jarie Bolander

The first time I showed up to a GORUCK training day was not long after I finished my first Ironman. I didn’t go looking for it. A friend from work dared me.

GORUCK is an endurance event where you pack a backpack full of bricks and take on challenges. Some involve getting cold, wet, and sandy. Others involve carrying odd-shaped objects around. The real events start at 10 p.m. and run until the sun comes up.

The training day was in daylight at Baker Beach in San Francisco, and it was all dudes. We had the same curiosity and the same burning desire to see what we were made of. We also wanted to find other knuckleheads who think spending time in the ocean at 2 a.m. is perfectly normal. Dare I say, fun.

What I didn’t know at the time was that some of the men I met on that beach would still be good friends of mine 14 years later. I wrote about those friendships in “The Power of Crucible Events to Solidify Male Friendships.”

That got me thinking about the origins of Movember.

Two Guys, a Beer, and a Dare

In 2003, two friends in Melbourne, Travis Garone and Luke Slattery, were having a beer at the Gypsy Bar in Fitzroy. The conversation drifted to fashion trends that keep coming back. They started wondering where the mustache had gone.

So they decided to bring it back. Travis emailed their friends with a subject line that doubled as a dare: “Are you man enough to be my man?”

Thirty guys said yes.

There was no cause that first year. No fundraising page. No awareness campaign. Just 30 men growing mustaches for a month.

The cause came the next year, when the group decided to grow for men’s health. Today, millions of men around the world take part.

Co-founder Adam Garone put it plainly: “Movember itself started with friends getting together, growing Mo’s and having fun.”

That’s the part that gets lost. Movember didn’t start as a health campaign that happened to involve friends. It started as a group of friends who happened to build a health campaign.

The dare came first.

Why Dumb Challenges Work

There’s a popular idea that men’s friendships are broken because men won’t open up. If guys would just talk about their feelings, the theory goes, the loneliness would lift.

Tyler Austin Harper isn’t buying it. Writing in The Atlantic, he argued that the real crisis of male friendship comes from something else. Men haven’t lost the ability to connect. They’ve lost the shared activities they connect through.

That fits what I’ve seen. Men don’t usually become friends sitting across a table and sharing. They become friends standing next to each other, doing something side by side.

It also takes time. A lot of it. University of Kansas researcher Jeffrey Hall estimates it takes 40 to 60 hours to form a casual friendship, and more than 200 hours to become good friends. And not all hours count the same. Hanging out and joking around builds friendship. Working together counts for much less.

That’s the hidden genius of a dumb challenge. It gives you hours together that feel like play. Nobody on that training day was on the clock. Nobody was networking. We were a bunch of guys carrying bricks around a beach because we wanted to.

A month of growing a mustache works the same way. It’s time with your friends you’d never think to schedule. It also shows your care for your fellow men.

The Excuse Is the Point

Movember gets this.

This year’s campaign is built around a simple message: Connection doesn’t have to be a big heart-to-heart.

As Movember’s marketing director, Helena Jennison, put it, “Connection doesn’t always have to start with a difficult conversation.” Sometimes it’s a laugh. Sometimes it’s a shared interest. Sometimes it’s growing a mustache.

It works. According to Movember’s own research, two in five people who took part made a new social connection through it.

The charity funds the same idea year-round. In Newcastle, England, a program called Men’s Pie Club starts from a simple premise. Men like eating pies. So they learn to make them together. The conversations come later, as the men get to know each other.

Look at what’s going on in each of these. Nobody signs up for “emotional connection.” They sign up for a mustache, a pie, a beach full of bricks. The activity is the excuse. The friendship is what they actually came for, even if they’d never say so.

Men need a reason to be in the same place at the same time. Give them one, and they’ll usually take it from there.

Find Your Knuckleheads

You don’t need a cause to start. You need a dare.

Here are three ways to find yours this month.

  1. Join or start a Movember team: It’s November. Grow a mustache with a few guys from work, the gym, or the soccer sideline. Thirty days of questionable facial hair gives you a built-in reason to check in every week.
  2. Sign up for something slightly ridiculous: A GORUCK event. A mud run. A polar plunge on New Year’s Day. Pick something hard enough that you’ll need the guys next to you, and dumb enough that you’ll laugh about it later.
  3. Send the email: That 2003 subject line still works. Pick five guys and dare them to do something with you. Some will ignore it. One or two won’t.

In my book, The Male Friendship Experience, I call these friendship missions: shared activities that give men a reason to show up, again and again. The mission matters less than the showing up.

Fourteen years ago, a work friend dared me to go carry bricks on a beach. I went to train. I found the men I’d later stand beside in the dark Pacific at 2 a.m. Those same men still stand by me on great days and dark days.

Be the guy who sends the dare.

item.title: Beyond the Snowflake Myth
item.description:
Adolescence

Beyond the Snowflake Myth

New research shows that young people are not "snowflakes" but culture-crushed.

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Attitudes towards young people's problems vary from sympathy to frustration.
  • A new report about supporting young people’s mental well-being challenges the snowflake myth.
  • Common diagnoses of autism and ADHD are often applied too easily, but that is not the end of the story.
  • Young people seek a diagnosis as the pathway to help, and we need to change this model.

“Snowflake generation” is a term applied to young people who are quickly overwhelmed or “melted” by commonplace pressures and challenges. The rise in young people’s mental health problems and diagnoses of conditions such as autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are sometimes put in this framework, whereby young people today are less resilient and robust than in previous generations of youth who navigated equally, if not more difficult, environments.

Shifting views of young people’s dependence

Getting a sound perspective on young people’s well-being is essential to assessing appropriate levels of support: How much do we help them by offering practical, emotional, financial and professional support, and how much does such support hinder their capacity to grow resilience themselves?

Across the past three decades, my views of young people’s challenges and how much support the grown-ups in their lives should offer have changed. At the beginning of this century, I wrote about the split between young people’s realities on the one hand and cultural expectations about maturity on the other. [1] I argued that expecting young people to be adults when they reach the age of legal adulthood was unrealistic and damaging—damaging because parents often felt disappointed or frustrated with what they saw as the delayed development of their children, and young people absorbed this disappointment. I pointed out that the conditions of young people today are thin on intergenerational social capital—a deep sense of belonging and a community on which they can draw for informal, personal support. Instead, they are left to get on with pressured social lives, rife with competition and little individually tailored input from teachers, preachers, neighbors or even relatives.

When I subsequently served as a dean in a Cambridge College, I witnessed new trends whereby young people were increasingly keen to label themselves with “special” needs. These involved a host of adjustments, from extra time for examinations and dedicated teaching tools to demands for modifying the entire syllabus to avoid “triggering” bad feelings. This was a time, too, when diagnoses of disabilities were rising rapidly. With more extensive screening for disabilities and broadening diagnostic criteria, the number of young people identified as dyslexic grew to more than 20 times from the baseline recorded in the 1990s by 2015, while cases of autism increased by 175 percent between 2011 and 2022. [1]

Like many people in educational institutions, I worried that young people were seeking a formal assessment of disability partly to obtain in-group status with a distinctive set and partly to demand additional input from their teachers. There was a risk that instead of taking on the task of learning how to learn, how to communicate and interact, how to accept the variability of their talents, young people were now primed to outsource their challenges, demanding that others make adjustments to spoon-feed and coddle them. As an increasing number of their peers sought more input and adjustments, it was common to feel that being mainstream or neurotypical meant being left out.

The reality of young people’s unmet needs

The UK government, concerned about the rise in young people’s mental health needs, ordered an investigation of young people’s mental health and appointed Peter Fonagy, clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England, to lead the research. I anticipated that the report would show that ordinary difficult feelings—anxiety, frustration, stress, pressure, uncertainty—were all too often pathologized as disorders or conditions when the best approach would be to support young people to manage normal ups and downs of human emotions.

The review of young people’s mental health showed something very different and has prompted another shift in my perspective—not because of my previous concern that some mental health and disability diagnoses are too broad, but because the charge of overdiagnosis, while valid, clouds the main issue that there has been a significant rise in mental distress among young people. This is affecting both boys and girls, but from the age of 12, the impact on girls is greater. The close-up view is heartbreaking: many young people struggle with anxiety so powerful that they find school intolerable. Some are too depressed to sleep or eat, and some feel their lives are “not worth living.” [2]

In reflecting on the report, Peter Fonagy said, “I am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”

The new UK review complements the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2023 report finding that nearly three out of five teen girls experience persistent sadness, double that in boys. [3] Misery and a sense of being weird, disliked, and also very special might be a signature element of adolescence, but today’s adolescence is crushing our children, who inhabit a digital ecosystem that inflicts persistent social comparison and self-doubt, socioeconomic instability and a precarious future, and a fractured support system that incentivizes the search for a special diagnosis because that is the route through which they might begin to get professional support.

I have circled back to my conviction that we need to offer sympathy and understanding and proactive support to young people—in the home, in school and in the community—to meet their core needs for autonomy (confidence in navigating risk), competence (skills to succeed academically and socially), and relatedness (belonging, community and purpose). Only with our support will these challenged generations of youth discover resilience.

item.title: What Stressed Teens Need During College Application Season
item.description:
Adolescence

What Stressed Teens Need During College Application Season

“If I don’t get into a good college, my life will be ruined.”

Posted November 6, 2026

Key points
  • Academic pressure is real, widespread, and can harm teens' mental health.
  • Well-meant parental advice to reduce stress can feel to teens like more pressure.
  • Start a conversation. Ask your teen, “How important do you think your grades are to me?” Then just listen.
  • A close parent-teen relationship is one of the strongest buffers against the impact of academic pressure.

“If I don’t get into a good college, my life will be ruined.”

In more than 30 years of working with adolescents, I’ve heard some version of this more times than I can count. I hear it especially often this time of year when high school seniors are working on college applications. I understood it differently, however, when the teenager overwhelmed by academic pressure was my own child.

During her senior year, my daughter was taking many AP classes and spending 20 hours a week on extracurricular activities. She was doing all this because she believed she had to get into a “good college.” She was often sleeping fewer than six hours a night, was increasingly irritable, had circles under her eyes, and seemed miserable.

My wife and I are both therapists. My wife specializes in stress management. So we did all the “right” things: we encouraged our daughter to sleep more, take breaks, see friends, study less, and try meditation.

She wasn’t interested. The more we pushed, the more she resisted. All we accomplished was a series of big fights, which cost her even more sleep and left her feeling even more stressed and further behind.

We wondered what we were doing wrong.

What we eventually realized was that sometimes the most helpful thing parents can do is stop trying to change their child’s experience long enough to understand it.

The pressure is real

The pressure driving my daughter wasn’t just in her head. It came from her friends, her school, and our town. The environment surrounding many of our teens is a pressure cooker.

In a survey of more than 270,000 high school students between 2010 and 2023, the nonprofit Challenge Success found that “students consistently report overall workload, homework, tests or quizzes, finals, and assessments as their top sources of stress.” In a 2023 scientific review, 48 of 52 studies reported a link between academic pressure and mental health problems in adolescents.

Drawing on her own research and that of others, psychologist Suniya Luthar wrote in 2020:

“Major policy reports now list students at high-achieving schools as an at-risk group, alongside children in poverty, those experiencing trauma, and those in foster care or with incarcerated parents.”

I couldn’t believe this when I first read it. Most of us think of attending a high-achieving school as an advantage, not a potential risk to a child’s mental health. Luthar continued:

“Rates of clinically significant anxiety and depression can be as high as six times the national norm in many high-achieving schools (HASs), where children’s mental health is severely affected by ongoing, ubiquitous, and unrelenting pressure to achieve.”

When our kids say they’re drowning at school, they’re not exaggerating.

Good advice that’s hard to follow

What should parents do about all this academic stress and pressure? Based on its research, Challenge Success recommends reducing “‘unnecessary stress’ stemming from factors such as unreasonably heavy course load, high levels of pressure around admittance to elite universities, and piling on of extracurricular activities for the primary purpose of building a college resume.”

They also recommend PDF: making sure kids take time for (P)laytime, (D)owntime, and (F)amily time.

This is excellent advice. It’s also almost exactly what my wife and I told our daughter. The problem often isn’t knowing what stressed teens need.

It’s that our help can feel like more pressure

Looking back, I could see that our daughter didn’t feel we understood what she was up against. To her, feeling unprepared for a test was way more stressful than losing sleep. Our attempts to get her to live a more balanced life felt like more pressure, not help.

Many parents are similarly surprised by how their interest comes across. A 2014 Harvard survey of more than 10,000 middle and high school students found that three times as many agreed with the statement, “My parents are prouder if I get good grades in my classes than if I’m a caring community member in class and school,” than disagreed with it.

Teens are highly sensitive to evaluation, and when so many of our questions to them are about tests and assignments, it’s easy for them to experience our interest in school as if it’s all we care about.

This gap between what we mean and what our kids hear is why checking in with them matters so much.

Ask this question

Pick a calm moment, not right after a bad grade or in the middle of a particularly stressful week, and ask your teen: “How important do you think your grades are to me?” Then just listen.

This question brings into the open something that your teen may already believe but might not say. Asking communicates that you care about how they experience you, that you are open to feedback, and that you are interested in more than their grades. Hopefully, it also invites a conversation.

The hardest part isn’t asking the question; it’s being open to the answer. Your teen may say something that surprises or stings: “You only care about my grades” or “Nothing I do is ever good enough.” Their picture of you may feel unfair, or even distorted. Resist the urge to correct them. The moment you defend yourself, the conversation ends.

Instead, stay curious: “Tell me more. What makes you feel that way?” When they’ve finished, say back to them what you heard and check whether you’ve understood: “Do you feel like I get it?” If not, ask, “What am I missing?” Your goal isn’t to convince your teen that they’re wrong. It’s to understand why they see things that way.

Paradoxically, feeling understood and validated is what makes people open to seeing things differently. You may not change how your teen sees you in one conversation, but you’ll have shown them that you’re on their side.

Keep the door open

A close, supportive relationship with parents is one of the most consistent protective factors for teens’ mental health. Asking the question opens the door. A few everyday habits keep it open:

  • Ask permission before offering solutions. “Would it help if I shared an idea?” Giving your teen control over when and how they get your input actually makes them more receptive to it.
  • Have 25 one-minute conversations instead of one 25-minute one. Many teens resist long, serious talks. Short check-ins that end on a good note build momentum without feeling like an interrogation.
  • Talk about things other than school. Ask about their friends, their music, what shows they’re watching. Every non-academic conversation reinforces that you care about who they are, not just what they achieve.

When it’s more than stress

Some stress is normal. It can be a sign we’re challenging ourselves. However, if your teen shows sadness, irritability, or hopelessness lasting more than two weeks, withdraws from normal activities, has big changes in sleep or appetite, or says anything about self-harm or not wanting to be alive, it’s time to get help. Reach out to your pediatrician or a mental health professional immediately.

The takeaway

With our daughter, we stopped trying to force stress management on her and pivoted to listening to what she was going through. We asked her the question, and her answer surprised us. She didn’t feel that her grades were all we cared about. She needed us to understand how important they were to her. Once we did, our relationship got better. She kept pushing herself, but over time, she came to see us as a reliable source of support and not pressure.

We can’t remove the pressure our kids face, but we can make sure we’re not adding to the load. Our relationship with our kids is one of the best buffers against the negative impact of academic pressure, and it’s the thing that pressure most often erodes, as it did in my house. Protecting our relationship is the most important thing we can do for our children. Not so they’ll perform better, but so they can thrive.​
